candidates.statement: The FDA guidance for industry Optimizing the Dosage of Human Prescription Drugs and 73 Biological Products for the Treatment of Oncologic Diseases (August 2024) contrasts the 74 historical dosage selection for cytotoxic chemotherapies, where the maximum tolerated dose 75 (MTD) was identified in dose-finding trials and frequently administered in subsequent clinical 76 trials, to that of modern targeted oncology drugs where dosages below the MTD may have 77 similar efficacy to the MTD with fewer toxicities. RPTs share characteristics with both cytotoxic 78 chemotherapies and modern targeted oncology drugs, and the MTD of many RPTs with respect 79 to either acute or long-term toxicities has not been established at least in part due to prior 80 adherence to EBRT organ tolerances. Therefore, it is not yet clear whether identifying an MTD 81 (or dosing up to normal tissue tolerances) is the optimal approach for determining the 82 recommended dosage for an RPT. Furthermore, the appropriateness of an MTD-based dosing 83 strategy may be product- and situation-specific and could depend on numerous factors (e.g., 84 target expression, ligand specificity, physical properties of the isotope and construct [stability, 85 half-life, and decay scheme]; and slopes of the dose-response and dose-toxicity relationships for 86 a given participant population). Although determination of the MTD may provide useful 87 information, dosages selected for trials intended to support a future marketing application should 88 be based on a totality of available data from a range of dosages, and not based solely on the 89 MTD or normal organ tolerances. 90

candidates.statement: Administered activities per cycle and/or cumulative RPT administered activities that result in 95 tissue absorbed doses that exceed EBRT organ tolerances or previously characterized RPT 96 dosages may be studied in clinical trials of RPTs when there is adequate rationale that the 97 optimized dose of an RPT may not be identified at lower dosages (i.e., dosages that do not 98 exceed EBRT organ tolerances or previously characterized RPT dosages). Proposals to expose 99 participants to RPT dosages that exceed EBRT organ tolerances or previously characterized RPT 100 dosages could be justified based on existing clinical data or other approaches, as applicable, and 101 should be discussed with FDA during formal meetings, including early in clinical development. 102 Trials should include safeguards such as appropriate participant selection, trial design, safety 103 monitoring, and radiation dosimetry evaluation. 104

candidates.statement: • RPTs should generally be administered for a fixed number of cycles to mitigate the risk 148 of delayed or cumulative toxicity. Protocols should pre-specify a limit to the cumulative 149 administered activity, and corresponding radiation absorbed doses to critical organs, that 150 is justified based on available data on RPT-specific organ tolerances. The appropriate 151 limit may be product- and indication-specific, and the appropriate limits may be revised 152 based on emerging data. In situations where there is relatively high uncertainty (e.g., a 153 novel product with no clinical data, alpha-emitter RPTs, RPTs that are predicted to have 154 heterogeneous sub-organ distribution of radiation, or existence of uncertainties about 155 additive toxicity from prior RPT treatment), a lower limit to cumulative activity delivered 156 in a particular protocol may be appropriate as a starting point. In situations where there is 157 less uncertainty (e.g., established product with substantial clinical data, high-energy beta- 158 emitting isotopes, RPTs with relatively homogeneous sub-organ distribution of radiation, 159

candidates.statement: — While a DLT period of one cycle may be sufficient to allow escalation to a higher 187 dose in initial dose-finding trials, sponsors should incorporate longer-term safety 188 and tolerability data into their decision-making to justify the recommended 189 dosage(s) for subsequent trials. If multiple cycles of an RPT are intended, safety 190 data obtained with one cycle will not be sufficient to support a dosage for future 191 development; in this case, safety data from participants who received multiple 192 cycles and from multiple dose levels should be provided to assess potential 193 cumulative toxicity. The choice of a recommended dosage(s) for trials intended to 194 support a future marketing application should be informed by a duration of safety 195 follow-up that corresponds to the timeframe of the anticipated toxicities, and/or 196 the median life expectancy of the participant population (if less than the 197 timeframe of anticipated long-term toxicities). 198

candidates.statement: — Sponsors should compare multiple dosages, including in randomized dose- 208 response trials, prior to selecting a dosage(s) for trials intended to support a future 209 marketing application, given that the optimized dosage may or may not 210 correspond to the highest dose studied. Randomized dose-response trials may be 211 particularly important when evaluating a dosage(s) that exceeds EBRT-defined 212 organ tolerances, or a dosage(s) that corresponds to the MTD of an RPT. 213 Randomized dose-response trials should be sized to allow for adequate 214 assessment of activity, safety, and tolerability for each dosage. Refer to the FDA 215 guidance for industry Optimizing the Dosage of Human Prescription Drugs and 216 Biological Products for the Treatment of Oncologic Diseases (August 2024) for 217 general information on randomized parallel dose-response trials. The dosage(s) 218 selected for trials intended to support a future marketing application should be 219 based both on data from randomized dose-response trials, including preliminary 220 efficacy and shorter-term toxicity data, as well as longer-term toxicity data 221 available from the initial dose-finding trial(s), including any backfilled cohorts. 222

candidates.statement: • Because the onset of radiation toxicity may be delayed by months to years, sponsors 237 should perform monitoring against a pre-specified list of late radiation adverse events of 238 special interest (rAESI) for at least 5 years after the last dose or until death in cases where 239 life expectancy is typically expected to be less than 5 years. The rAESI list and 240 monitoring schedule should explicitly reflect the drug-specific dosimetry results and a 241 corresponding detailed critical radiation safety analysis plan. RPTs granted approval for 242 cancer indications may be subject to a postmarketing requirement to provide such long- 243 term safety follow-up data for FDA review. 244

candidates.statement: • Per 21 CFR 312.23(a)(10)(ii), phase 1 studies of radioactive drugs must include studies 261 which will obtain sufficient data for dosimetry calculations. Each novel molecular entity 262 should have dosimetry studies performed early in its clinical development program to 263 provide measurements of potential toxicity/efficacy associated with exposure to radiation 264 (e.g., delivered organ absorbed dose and related dosimetric quantities). Dosimetry studies 265 provide a radiobiological context for the clinical efficacy and safety data and support 266 dosage optimization. Given that the properties (e.g., physical and effective half-life, 267 decay products and associated energies) of different radioisotopes vary widely, the 268 appropriate design of the dosimetry studies may be isotope- or product-specific. Direct 269 imaging of the therapeutic product is preferred, when possible, although this may be 270 supplemented by dosimetry data from surrogate analogs when direct imaging is not 271 possible or has substantial limitations. 272
candidates.context: D. Dosimetry for Dosage Optimization Trials 259 • If an Investigational New Drug (IND) submission is supported by data obtained from 274 studies that were not conducted under an IND and did not obtain dosimetry data, FDA 275 expects that dosimetry data will be obtained during the trial included in the original IND 276 submission to verify assumptions made in dosage selection. This could be accomplished 277 via a dedicated imaging study or a lead-in cohort. In these situations, sponsors should 278 request a meeting with the appropriate FDA division to discuss the dosimetry data prior 279 to enrolling a large number of participants in a trial intended to support a future 280 marketing application. 281
